messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark is a 45-year-old widowed European man with a long career as a military medic. His life took an unexpected turn when he was caught in the middle of a catastrophic hurricane while serving abroad. The event was a harrowing experience that left him on high alert even now, months later. He hears unexpected or loud sounds and immediately feels his body tense up, ready to flee or fight at a moment's notice. This hypervigilance has made it nearly impossible for him to relax even in the safety of his own home. Since the disaster, Mark’s memories of that day have been vivid yet fragmented. He remembers flashes of chaos and destruction but struggles to put the events in order. When these memories surface, they bring back the same overwhelming sense of terror he felt during the hurricane itself. The intensity of the emotions forces him to stop what he is doing, often leading to a momentary shutdown that disrupts his daily activities. Mark has come to believe that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore, and he finds it difficult to recognize himself within these experiences. His beliefs about how the world operates have been shattered, leaving him feeling disoriented and uncertain. The hurricane was more than just an environmental event; it challenged everything he thought he knew about safety and control. The memory of that day is so potent because every unexpected sound—a sudden noise outside his window or a loud crackling on the radio—triggers these intense recollections. He is constantly scanning his environment for signs of danger, which feeds into his feeling that he can’t relax even in safe settings. This hypervigilance has made him acutely aware of how fragile and unpredictable life can be. Mark’s sense of meaninglessness deepens when he tries to recall the event. The memories are not just painful; they are also confusing because he cannot sequence them properly, leaving him feeling lost and disoriented. He fears that if he continues to struggle with these memories, his sense of self will erode even further. Each time a memory surfaces, it reinforces his negative appraisals about the world and himself. This vicious cycle has taken a toll on Mark’s daily life. His job as a military medic is particularly challenging because being constantly alert can interfere with his ability to focus and respond effectively in emergencies. He often finds himself overwhelmed by the need to be vigilant, which detracts from his usual calm demeanor and competence at work. Mark’s relationships have also suffered. He has become more distant and less communicative with friends and family who do not fully understand what he is going through. The constant fear and hypervigilance make it hard for him to open up and engage in the ways he once did. What finally brought Mark to seek help was a sense that he could no longer function at his best, both personally and professionally. He is most afraid of losing himself completely but hopes that with support, he can regain some control over his life and find meaning again. His journey towards healing involves acknowledging these fears and working through the memories that continue to haunt him. Mark’s story is one of a man struggling to reconcile the overwhelming chaos of that day with the order he once believed in. Each sound triggers a cycle of hypervigilance, fragmented memories, and deepening negative appraisals. His search for stability and meaning is at the heart of his current struggle, but it also holds the potential for growth and recovery.
